exam: A 45‑year‑old woman with BMI 28 kg/m² has a 2‑hour OGTT of 165 mg/dL. What is the diagnosis and next step? — Impaired glucose tolerance; advise lifestyle changes and schedule repeat testing in 6‑12 months.
How does impaired glucose tolerance differ from impaired fasting glucose in pathophysiology? — IGT reflects peripheral insulin resistance; IFG reflects hepatic insulin resistance.

A patient on rifampicin for TB shows a 2‑hour OGTT of 150 mg/dL. How does TB treatment affect interpretation? — Rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes, may lower drug levels but does not cause hyperglycaemia; repeat OGTT after TB completion.

Why is metformin preferred over sulfonylureas for IGT in low‑resource settings? — Metformin has low hypoglycaemia risk and is inexpensive; sulfonylureas can cause dangerous hypoglycaemia without close monitoring.

What lifestyle advice would you give a farmer with IGT who cannot afford a gym? — Encourage brisk walking 30 min daily, use field work as exercise, limit sugary drinks, eat more whole grains and legumes.
A pregnant woman has a 2‑hour OGTT of 155 mg/dL. How does this affect management? — Indicates gestational diabetes risk; refer for obstetric glucose monitoring and dietary counseling.
Explain why a single random glucose of 180 mg/dL does not confirm IGT. — Random glucose >200 mg/dL suggests diabetes; 180 mg/dL is inconclusive, requires OGTT or fasting glucose.
What are the cardiovascular implications of untreated IGT? — Increases risk of atherosclerosis, hypertension, and myocardial infarction; early intervention reduces events.
ai.title: Impaired Glucose Tolerance
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) is a pre‑diabetic state with 2‑hour post‑load glucose 140‑199 mg/dL. It signals high risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Often asymptomatic; may present with polyuria, fatigue after meals
Prevalence rising with urbanisation and obesity in East Africa
sections.p: IGT reflects defective peripheral glucose uptake after a carbohydrate challenge. It is identified by an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) when fasting glucose is <126 mg/dL but 2‑hour glucose is 140‑199 mg/dL.

t.b: Is there overt diabetes? – 100‑125 mg/dL supports pre‑diabetes; ≥126 mg/dL defines diabetes
What is long‑term glycaemia? – 5.7‑6.4 % indicates pre‑diabetes; ≥6.5 % defines diabetes

b: Insulin resistance > insulin secretory defect early in disease
Risk factors: obesity, sedentary life, family history, HIV‑ART, TB treatment steroids, malaria‑related inflammation
sections.p: IGT results from insulin resistance in muscle and delayed insulin secretion. It is a reversible stage if lifestyle and risk factors are addressed.

b: Screen high‑risk groups: BMI ≥ 25 kg/m², HIV on protease inhibitors, post‑TB treatment, pregnant women (gestational diabetes risk)
sections.p: Patients with IGT have a 5‑10 % annual progression to type 2 diabetes and higher cardiovascular mortality. Early detection allows preventive measures.

b: Emphasise lifestyle first, then metformin if progression risk high
sections.p: Examiners may ask you to interpret OGTT results, differentiate IGT from diabetes, and outline management in a low‑resource setting.

b: Do not start insulin for IGT alone
Do not dismiss a normal fasting glucose if 2‑hour OGTT is high
sections.p: Pitfalls include treating IGT as diabetes, ignoring fasting glucose, and relying on a single random glucose measurement.
Use simple, affordable tests; when unavailable, substitute with clinical risk scores.

t.b: Is there overt hyperglycaemia? – >200 mg/dL suggests diabetes; normal does not rule out IGT
What is the obesity risk? – BMI ≥ 25 kg/m² or waist >94 cm (men) / >80 cm (women) supports IGT risk
Is there glucosuria? – Positive may indicate diabetes; negative does not exclude IGT

b: Diet: 5‑6 small meals, limit simple carbs, increase fibre, reduce saturated fat
Metformin (if available) – improves insulin sensitivity, low hypoglycaemia risk; avoid sulfonylureas due to hypoglycaemia
sections.p: First‑line is lifestyle modification; metformin is added only if progression risk is high or lifestyle fails.
Distinguish IGT from impaired fasting glucose (IFG) and overt diabetes.

b: Repeat OGTT after recovery from infection
sections.p: Acute illness, malaria or HIV can transiently raise glucose, giving false‑positive IGT.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent polyuria/polydipsia with random glucose >200 mg/dL
Signs of ketoacidosis (vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing)
